candidates.title: TANK 5 Pro Puts Thermal Imaging and a 2K Projector in a Rugged Phone
candidates.full_text:
A phone that can spot a warm patch around a window and project a diagram onto a wall has a different idea of being useful. The 8849 TANK 5 Pro brings thermal imaging and a 2K projector into a rugged smartphone, keeping tools for investigating, recording, and sharing together. You can check something, save what you find, then let everyone else see it without crowding around the screen.

That starts with the FLIR Lepton 3.1R thermal camera, which records surface-temperature differences rather than ordinary photographs. Its native 160×120 resolution comes with a 95° horizontal field of view, useful for framing more of an electrical cabinet or a section of wall from nearby. MyFLIR Pro provides spot and area measurements to help you compare warmer and cooler parts of the scene.

Of course, a heat pattern only tells part of the story. A 50MP main camera lets you record the surrounding details, while a separate 50MP infrared night-vision camera helps when visible light is scarce. There’s also a 50MP telephoto camera for tighter framing and a 32MP front camera for calls. Keeping these different views on one device makes documenting an inspection a straightforward process.

The screen becomes a shared workspace for those different views. A 6.73-inch 3K AMOLED panel combines a 1440×3200 resolution with a 120Hz refresh rate, providing detail for reviewing photographs and smoother scrolling through maps. Its manufacturer-rated peak brightness reaches 3,000 nits, a useful specification when the next thing you need to check is outside rather than under office lighting.

Sharing those details doesn’t have to involve passing the phone around. Its built-in DLP projector offers 2K output at 2048×1080, with rated brightness of 220 lumens and laser autofocus. In a dim room or even with the lights on during the day, a wall becomes somewhere to discuss a floor plan or review photographs together. Later, the same hardware can put a movie on that wall without packing a separate projector.

There’s another way to share when a monitor is already nearby. DisplayPort 1.4 Alt Mode over USB-C supports external display output up to 4K through compatible equipment. That gives the phone two distinct ways to make information visible to a group: project onto a suitable surface, or connect to an existing screen. Either way, there’s no need to transfer your files to a presentation computer first.

Behind those specialized tools sits familiar smartphone hardware. Android 16 runs on MediaTek’s Dimensity 9400e, paired here with 18GB of physical RAM and 512GB of storage. That combination gives maps, inspection apps, photographs, and documents a common home, with room to keep reference material alongside what you’ve captured. You can open the relevant app on the same device that collected the information.

The phone can also move between connections as your day changes. There’s 5G away from a router and Wi-Fi 7 for compatible networks, while eSIM support adds another way to manage a supported mobile plan. For someone traveling between locations, that means an option beyond swapping physical SIM cards. Sending a report or downloading a revised drawing remains part of the same phone-based routine.

The physical controls deserve some attention, too. Programmable side keys let you assign selected functions to buttons, putting frequently used tools a button press away instead of behind another set of menus. The integrated camping light offers a separate source of illumination when you’re checking equipment or sorting gear after sunset. Alongside its rugged enclosure, these details give the phone a purpose that extends beyond its touchscreen.

All of that hardware shares a 17,600mAh battery, with support for up to 120W wired charging and a fast charger included in the box. The capacity makes particular sense alongside a projector and an integrated light, features that ask a phone to keep working after its screen would normally go dark. Back at an outlet, charging becomes part of getting the kit ready, alongside packing cables and checking tomorrow’s route.

candidates.title: Epomaker RT100 Pro swaps its numpad screen for four keys and keeps the knob
candidates.full_text:
Epomaker’s RT100 Pro lets buyers delete the screen from their keyboard and take four plain keys instead. It’s an odd trade. The 1.54-inch TFT module sits beside the numpad on this 1800-layout board, and the four-key cluster drops into the same slot.

Price : From $91.19 Where to buy : Buy on Amazon

The board sells for $98.59 at Epomaker’s store , marked down from $115.99, and Amazon’s listing starts at $91.19. Under a hundred either way.

Epomaker sells the board in Retro White and Pink, with the screen fitted in the photos and the key cluster as the alternate build. Both colors carry the same hardware. Only the corner module and the keycap colors change between them. Shipping runs worldwide from the maker’s store. The first RT100 got a full review here in 2023.

On the screen sits the clock, the battery level, the connection mode, and any GIF loaded onto it. The key cluster trades the display for four dedicated keys that just work. Neither setup costs extra. Epomaker builds the board around the swappable module, so the choice happens by configuration rather than by model. The module also decides the desk’s look from across the room.

A programmable metal knob survives both layouts, mapped to volume out of the box and reassignable in the software to zoom, scroll, or brush sizes. It’s the one part nobody trades away.

It also mirrors system info during a session, and the GIF support turns it into a tiny loop of whatever gets uploaded. It’s decoration with a job. The keys answer with muscle memory instead, no glance down required.

The 1800 layout squeezes a full numpad and a function row into a footprint of 43.3 by 14.2 centimeters. That’s 103 keys plus the module corner. Arrow keys and the navigation cluster tuck under the right side of the board. Desks keep some breathing room. The function row survives the squeeze too, which smaller layouts usually sacrifice first.

Weight lands at about 1.3 kilograms, with a fixed 5.8-degree typing angle in an ABS case with a gasket-mounted plate inside. A PC plate and Cherry-profile dye-sub PBT keycaps finish the build without a metal case’s price tag.

At 4.5 centimeters thick before the keycaps, it sits tall on a desk and looks like a full-size board from across the room. Smaller boards look lost next to it. The weight helps there, since 1.3 kilograms doesn’t slide around during fast typing.

Six layers of dampening sit under the gasket-mounted plate, from PORON foam at the top to a silicone sheet at the bottom. The stack targets the hollow ping that thin plastic boards can’t hide at this price. Switch choice splits two ways. Creamy Jade linears run 45 grams of actuation force, and the Sea Salt Silent V2 linears keep the same weight behind silent stems.

Both switch options come factory-lubed, and the sockets take any 3-pin or 5-pin switch for later swaps. Connectivity covers USB-C, 2.4 GHz wireless, and Bluetooth across five paired devices. Polling hits 1,000 Hz wired and over the dongle, with latency as low as 4 milliseconds on a cable.

Battery capacity is 5,000 mAh. It feeds the tri-mode radios and the south-facing per-key RGB, and the LEDs aim the glow at the typist while the dye-sub legends stay readable under it.

Buy it if the desk runs on spreadsheets and shortcuts, because the numpad and the knob earn their space daily on a working desk. Skip it if a 65% board already covers the workload. Wait for the Sea Salt Silent version if the office shares walls, because the silent stems are the quiet half of this lineup. Both builds cost the same. This one’s for the spreadsheet-heavy typer who still wants a board with some personality left in it.

Budget shoppers should run the Amazon listing first, since its starting price undercuts the maker’s sale price by about seven dollars. The maker’s store counters with both switch options, both module builds and the full color range. That’s real money at this end of the market.

Price : From $91.19 Where to buy : Buy on Amazon

The catch is the fixed angle: the 5.8-degree tilt doesn’t adjust, and there’s no wrist rest in the box. Extra Mac keycaps do come in the box, and the board runs on Windows, Mac, and Android without a driver hunt or a dongle drawer.

candidates.title: Forgotten Lampshades Become Playful Chandeliers in This Romanian Designer’s Lighting Collection
candidates.full_text:
There is something undeniably charming about objects that carry traces of the past. Their imperfections, unusual proportions, and familiar textures often hold a character that contemporary manufacturing struggles to recreate. With Lampa Volta, Romanian designer Mihai Popescu embraces this character, transforming forgotten lampshades into a lighting collection that feels earthy, expressive, and quietly luxurious. What began as a fascination with discarded objects has evolved into a celebration of craftsmanship, materiality, and the beauty of giving old things new purpose.

The collection draws inspiration from an extraordinary archive of more than 300 vintage lampshades gathered over five years. Rather than treating these pieces as remnants of outdated design, Popescu recognized their potential to become part of something entirely new. Each lampshade carries its own visual identity, with shapes, colors, and details that reflect different periods of design. Bringing these elements together creates an intriguing conversation between past and present, where familiar forms find unexpected relevance in contemporary interiors.

Designer: Mihai Popescu Studio SRL , Romania

At the heart of Lampa Volta is a rich exploration of materials. Recycled elements sit alongside Murano glass, crystal tubes, and brass details, creating a composition that balances refinement with an organic, almost nostalgic warmth. The collection also incorporates glass blown by hand by Romanian artisan Jeni Costachescu, introducing another layer of craftsmanship to an already tactile design. The meeting of these materials gives each lighting piece a distinct personality, with delicate transparency, metallic accents, and vintage forms working together in a carefully considered arrangement.

What makes Lampa Volta particularly compelling is its interpretation of luxury. There is no attempt to make every element appear identical or perfectly uniform. Instead, the collection finds sophistication in variation, allowing different materials and forms to retain their individuality. Glass brings a sense of delicacy, crystal introduces a subtle brilliance, and brass contributes warmth and visual depth. Together, these elements create an atmosphere that feels collected and lived in rather than overly polished. It is a kind of luxury rooted in character, where the story behind an object becomes just as valuable as its appearance.

The earthy quality of the collection emerges through this relationship between materials, history, and craftsmanship. Although glass and crystal are often associated with ornate interiors, their combination with repurposed elements gives Lampa Volta a more grounded presence. The designs feel equally suited to a thoughtfully curated home or a hospitality space seeking an intimate, distinctive atmosphere. Their sculptural compositions make them compelling even when they are not illuminated, allowing them to function as decorative objects throughout the day.

Versatility is another defining quality of the collection. Lampa Volta is conceived as a family of lighting objects available in wall lamp, pendant, and chandelier configurations. Its shapes and colors can be endlessly rearranged, allowing the same design language to take on different expressions depending on the space. A smaller arrangement might lend warmth and personality to a residential corner, while a more elaborate chandelier could become the centerpiece of a restaurant, hotel, or public interior. This flexibility gives the collection room to evolve without losing its recognizable identity.

Beyond its visual appeal, Lampa Volta offers an interesting perspective on the relationship between sustainability and collectible design. Repurposing existing lampshades preserves objects that might otherwise be discarded, while the introduction of new materials and traditional glassmaking techniques extends their relevance. Rather than presenting reuse as an aesthetic compromise, the collection makes it central to its appeal. The result feels intentional and contemporary, with the history of each component contributing to the richness of the finished piece.

Lampa Volta invites a different way of looking at the objects around us. A forgotten lampshade becomes part of a sculptural arrangement, an old material finds new companionship, and the familiar glow of a lamp takes on an entirely different meaning.
